newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer implores jury to rule against Simpson.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer implores jury to rule against Simpson.

text.p: An attorney told jurors on Tuesday that O.J. Simpson's ex-wife and her friend were speaking to them "from the grave" and pointing to the former football star as their killer.

In an impassioned final summation at Simpson's civil trial, Daniel Petrocelli, the lead attorney for the victims' families, exhorted jurors to find him responsible for the killings, branding him "a guilty man, a man with no remorse, a man with no conscience."

Petrocelli contended Simpson offered no explanation for the mass of blood and DNA evidence linking him to the crime and lied repeatedly on the witness stand. Simpson, acquitted on Oct. 3, 1995, in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, is battling a wrongful-death civil lawsuit brought by the victims' families.
If he is found responsible for the June 1994 murders, he cannot be punished with jail but he could be forced to pay millions in damages.

As the trial moved toward a conclusion, both sides were confronted with the same daunting challenge: to piece together the puzzle of three months of testimony and create a compelling case for the jury.
Petrocelli, the first of three plaintiffs' lawyers who are to make presentations before the defence gets its chance on Wednesday, began his argument with a dramatic flourish.

"The critical pieces of evidence are ... the voices of Nicole and Ron speaking to us from the grave, telling us that there is a killer in this courtroom," Petrocelli said, pointing his finger at Simpson, seated across the room.

Holding that pose, he declared: "That is the man who confronted them, attacked them and killed them, the defendant, Orenthal James Simpson." He said the victims "in their last struggling moments to stay alive provided us with the key evidence necessary to identify their killer."

The glove and knit cap the attacker left at the murder scene, fingernail marks and cuts the victims allegedly left on Simpson's hand and the bloody shoeprints that led away from the bodies were ample proof of Simpson's guilt, he said.

Petrocelli said Goldman, a waiter and aspiring model who would have been 29, had planned to open his own restaurant. Nicole Brown Simpson would have been 37 and, on a day like this, making breakfast for her two young children and then driving them to school.
"But ... their lives came to a sudden end in a few moments of uncontrollable rage," he said.
To drive home the image, he showed the jury an enlarged photo of Nicole Brown Simpson's body lying in a pool of blood outside her Brentwood condominium.

Simpson's attorneys were expected to hammer on a theme that proved successful in the criminal case -- that he was falsely implicated by police who botched the murder investigation and planted and contaminated vital evidence.
Simpson lead attorney Robert Baker was expected to take the lectern on Wednesday. Petrocelli will then get the last word in rebuttal and the case could be in the jury's hands by Thursday afternoon.

Unlike the criminal trial, which required "proof beyond a reasonable doubt," the plaintiffs in the civil trial will prevail if they can prove there is a 50.1 percent probability -- a "preponderance of the evidence" -- that Simpson committed the murders. Only nine of the 12 jurors' votes are required.
